study.title: Leviticus 3 The Peaceful Sacrifice and Communion with God
study.overview: Leviticus 3 regulates the peaceful offering, also called the offer of communion. The chapter shows that this offering is centered not only on the atonement, but also on the restored and celebrated relationship between the Lord and his people. It could come from cattle, sheep or goats, always without defect, and involved the imposition of the hand, the slaughter of the animal, the blood sprinkled on the altar, and the burning of fat to the LORD. The text concludes with a perpetual prohibition: neither fat nor blood should be eaten, marking that life and the best part belong to God.

outline.title: Peaceful offer of vacum cattle
outline.explanation: The offer could be a male or a female of the cattle herd, but without defect. The offerer laid his hand on the head of the animal, which was knocked down at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony. The blood was sprinkled around the altar, and the inner fat, the kidneys and the fat bound to them were burnt offering to the LORD, on the burnt offering that was already on the altar.

outline.title: Peaceful offer of sheep
outline.explanation: When the offering came from the flock of sheep, the demands were very similar. The animal should also be without macula, with imposition of the hand, shedding blood and burning the fat, including the entire tail of the lamb. The text highlights that this portion was food of offering to the LORD, that is, something consecrated to him in worship.

outline.title: Peaceful goat offer and final ban
outline.explanation: The same structure appears to the goat: hand on the head, slaughter before the tent, sprinkled blood, and the burning of the fat on the altar. The final verse closes the chapter with a perpetual statute for all generations and in all dwellings: fat or blood should not be eaten.

study.context: The chapter integrates the instructions given to Israel for worship in the tabernacle, with priestly mediation. The repetition of the formulas shows care to order worship according to the divine commandment. The notes provided observe that the peaceful offer could express thanks, voluntarity or fulfillment of vow, and that often came after the burnt offering, suggesting that communion with God was based on the previous reality of atonement and consecration.
study.theology: Theologically, the peaceful offering expresses communion, reconciliation and joy before God. It is not only a sacrifice to withdraw from guilt, but a celebration of peace between the Lord and his people. The division of the sacrifice between the altar, the priest and the offerer points to participation in the presence of God, without confusing God with the human meal. The fat represents the richest and most precious part of the animal and is reserved for the Lord, which teaches that the best belongs to it. The prohibition of eating blood points out that life belongs to God and that blood has special value before him. In evangelical Christian reading, some commentators see in this sacrifice a figure of Christ's work, which promotes peace with God and produces a response of praise, gratitude and prayer; this is an interpretation, not an explicit statement of the verse.

scholarViews.insight: The peaceful offering expresses communion and well-being with the LORD, not only absence of conflict, but a shared meal in a sign of peace and friendship.
The repetition of the instructions for each type of animal shows God's zeal for the service to be done exactly according to its will, and reinforces the need for careful instruction in worship.

The rite of the imposition of the hand on the offering is explained as a figure of reconciliation, and the peaceful sacrifice is understood as a sign of the work of Christ that brings peace and also of the human response of praise and gratitude.

questions: What does the peaceful offering teach about worship as communion, and not just as a request for forgiveness?
What practical meaning does the LORD have to set aside and not to consume blood?
How can our life of worship today reflect gratitude, peace with God and reverence to what belongs to you?
study.practice: Apply this chapter by cultivating a spirituality of gratitude and communion: it approaches God by recognizing that peace with him is your gift, not human conquest; offer him the best of his time, resources and attention, not only leftovers; and treat life, holiness and worship with reverence, avoiding trivializing that which belongs to the LORD. It is also worth examining whether your faith produces concrete reconciliation with other people, since the peaceful offering points to peace received and shared.
